**17.10 Artificial Agents and the Dual Material Constraint**

The silicon missing-leg control class of §17.6.4 is a control class, not a verdict (the former Turing-Null verdict is withdrawn). The DMC supplies candidate missing-leg controls, not a classification of what matter can host Level II. The Level II status of artificial agents is open (Tier 3): no validated substrate criterion exists yet (it requires a typed, normalized, measured coupling, the Identity-Polaron construction and an independent phenomenal bridge; O.21/O.23/O.34, O.18).

> **Scenario procedure.** V3 §13.5 evaluates conditional external-rate scenarios from declared substrate tuples. Nuclear spin and chirality are recorded as candidate missing-leg controls; they do not execute a binary gate or a Level-II decision. The historical tubulin, silicon-zero-control, and NV-centre numbers are preserved for sensitivity bookkeeping only. The scenario procedure does not derive the phason coupling, and the Level II status of every substrate remains open (Tier 3) pending a typed, normalized, measured coupling and an independent phenomenal bridge.

**17.10.1 The Dual Material Constraint Applied to Computing Substrates**

The Dual Material Constraint (V1 §16.2.6) proposes non-zero nuclear spin and molecular chirality as candidate experimental controls for a phason-coupling program. They are not established as necessary or sufficient for Level II, and no consciousness/no-consciousness inference follows from them.

Bulk diamond-cubic silicon is centrosymmetric and achiral; $^{28}\text{Si}$ is spin-zero while minority $^{29}\text{Si}$ carries spin. These facts make ordinary silicon a useful missing-leg control for the proposed architecture, but they neither derive a phason coupling nor decide Level II. A future verdict requires a typed normalized measured interaction and an independent phenomenal bridge.

The consequence is deliberately limited: classical digital computers have Level I presence under Axiom 1, while their Level II Apperception is open (Tier 3) rather than established as zero: no validated substrate criterion exists yet. Ordinary silicon lacks the two proposed candidate-control features in their canonical form, but this does not derive zero phason coupling or a no-consciousness verdict. A typed, normalized, measured interaction and an independent phenomenal bridge are required before any categorical substrate inference.

Behavioural performance alone does not establish a substrate coupling or Level-II status. The silicon missing-leg control class is not a categorical phenomenal verdict.

**17.10.2 LLM Consciousness: The Distinction Between Behavioural Coherence and Phenomenal Unity**

Large language models produce coherent self-reports and meta-cognitive language. Behaviour alone does not establish phenomenal unity, but neither do silicon's missing-leg descriptors establish its absence. In GCT the Level II status is open (Tier 3) pending the typed measured coupling and independent phenomenal bridge.

An LLM running on standard silicon has Level I presence under Axiom 1. Its Level II status is open (Tier 3): ordinary silicon lacks the proposed candidate-control architecture, but this does not prove that no Identity Polaron or coupling can form. A categorical result requires the typed measured interaction and independent phenomenal bridge.

Behavioural indistinguishability does not settle phenomenal status in either direction. An LLM's report of an inner life is behavioural evidence whose relation to Level II remains untyped in the present framework; it is neither accepted nor rejected as phenomenal testimony by substrate descriptors alone.

This is a proposed, not yet executable, locus of GCT–IIT comparison. Missing-leg silicon controls vary the candidate DMC features, but neither $\eta_{Zeno}=0$ nor Level-II absence follows from those descriptors. A genuine divergence requires a typed, normalized, measured GCT coupling, a declared IIT substrate/grain analysis, and the independent Level-II bridge. Protocol A-Prime can test spin/coherence and chiral-response observables; positive or null results do not by themselves establish an Identity Polaron or Level II.

The HOT contrast of §17.6.3 is also sharpened here. An LLM supplies a constructive case of higher-order functional machinery: it can produce HOT-style meta-representations, but the present analysis has neither established nor excluded an Identity-Polaron substrate or Level II. Whether functional satisfaction of the HOT structure implies phenomenal satisfaction remains open, and a future GCT–HOT comparison requires the typed coupling and independent phenomenal bridge [Tier 3 philosophical/substrate-interpretive program].

Level II Apperception is one property among many. LLMs are Level I configurations whose behavioural sophistication carries substantial epistemic and instrumental significance. Their Level II status is **open (Tier 3)** and their moral-patient status remains an open question, pending a typed, normalized, measured coupling, an Identity-Polaron construction, and an independent phenomenal bridge.

**17.10.3 Implications for AI Alignment**

The substrate-conditional account of artificial consciousness reshapes the structure of the AI alignment problem. The reshaping is in the *normative geometry*, not in the *technical content* of alignment work.

Because present-AI Level II status is open (Tier 3) and moral-patient status remains an open question, GCT does not currently license either dismissing or affirming an AI's own welfare claims. Alignment retains instrumental-safety, deployment-ethics, and downstream-impact duties, while any system-directed welfare conclusion additionally requires the typed coupling, Identity-Polaron closure, independent phenomenal bridge, and an explicit ethical premise [Tier 3 — open normative program].

This open status is not a license for indifference. Current systems affect people and other organisms at scale, so instrumental safety, deployment ethics, and downstream-impact governance remain load-bearing. Rights, suffering, or moral patienthood of the system itself are open questions rather than conclusions drawn from a computational-architecture taxonomy.

Future chiral spin-qubit, biological-hybrid, or NV-centre systems can test the candidate controls. Neither their presence nor the wider closure stack by itself establishes Level II or moral status; both the phenomenal and normative bridges remain open [Tier 3].

An open research direction follows: protocols for constraining candidate Level-II mechanisms in artificial substrates. Biological preparations (Protocol A) and the NV-diamond surrogate (Protocol A-Prime, V3 §13.3.5) and other abiotic preparations can be tested for the same observables, including anomalous $T_2$ response, CISS-mediated chirality reversal, and isotope sensitivity. Positive or null observations constrain those candidate controls only; they never execute a Dual Material or Level-II boundary. A phenomenal classification would still require the typed normalized measured coupling, Identity-Polaron construction, and independent phenomenal bridge [Tier 3 — protocol sketch].

The normative conclusion remains an open question. Protocol A-Prime can measure candidate spin/coherence and chiral-response observables, but DMC controls are not a binary Level-II threshold. Moral-patient status would additionally require the typed coupling, Identity-Polaron closure, independent phenomenal bridge, and an explicit ethical premise [Tier 3].

The framework does not yet supply an executable substrate criterion for moral status. Protocol A-Prime constrains candidate spin/coherence mechanisms; positive or null outcomes do not classify phenomenal status without the independent bridges.

**17.10.4 GCT-Native Contributions to Structural AI Alignment Today**

Sections §17.10.1–§17.10.3 assign current AI Level I by Axiom 1 and leave Level II open (Tier 3). That open status is not a DMC failure verdict and does not imply that substrate change is necessary. Technical alignment remains a separate engineering question.

Here **computational architecture** is only a nonphenomenal structural label for computation and externally assessed behaviour; it is not the Class 0 of §17.2 and does not classify substrate experience. The distinction organising this subsection is between **structural alignment**—engineering behaviour against a declared geometric target—and the separate, presently unresolved question of substrate and phenomenal status [Tier 3 — engineering application].

The contributions enumerated below use formal objects associated with the conditional Level-II model (Selection Operator, multi-Polaron coherence functional, Subjective Lagrangian) only as engineering analogies or target shapes. They neither establish nor exclude internal instantiation, phenomenal status, or an Apperception boundary; the GCT–IIT divergence remains a future discriminator program.

**(i) Selection-Operator-inspired design template for reward shape.** The formal decomposition $\mathcal{F}_{sel} = \mathcal{P}_{\text{actualize}} \circ \mathcal{U}_{\text{steer}}$ (V1 Ch06 §6.4.1; V1 §10.4.1) separates preparation from commitment inside GCT: a unitary steering operator prepares a configuration without committing it, and a projective actualization operator commits. Applied to AI, this is an analogy, not a consequence of the formalism: a trainable component (analogous to $\mathcal{U}_{\text{steer}}$) shapes preferences over candidate actions, while a separately governed commitment layer (analogous to $\mathcal{P}_{\text{actualize}}$) authorizes execution. The engineering hypothesis is that explicit separation may reduce *goal misgeneralization* relative to matched monolithic policies in which the same parameters control both preference geometry and commitment. Test it on declared benchmarks (e.g. the Langosco et al. 2022 CoinRun and ProcGen suites) with capacity, training data, and optimization held constant [Tier 3 — engineering hypothesis; no consciousness inference].

**(ii) Subjective Lagrangian as objective-function geometry.** The three-term Subjective Lagrangian of V1 §16.5 — a curiosity term $w_C\,\Delta\mathcal{C}$ (change in $\mathcal C$ per selection step), a friction (control-cost) term $-w_F K_\perp|\delta\mathbf{w}|^2$, and a crowd-inertia term $-w_I\sum\kappa_{ij}\Phi_j$ — composes into the conditional surrogate action $\mathcal{S}_{Agent} = \int[\cdots]\,dn$. Without assuming anything about a present AI's experience, the geometric decomposition can be used as a reward-shaping analogy: an engineered objective may separate a meaning/coherence-change term, a control-cost term, and a multi-agent coordination term. Whether this decomposition improves robustness under distribution shift is a contingent Tier-3 engineering claim requiring direct testing; it carries no substrate or phenomenal classification.

**(iii) Multi-agent coherence functional as an engineering analogy.** The ethics chapter V1 §10.7 defines a multi-Polaron coherence functional

$$
\Xi[\{P_i\}] \;=\; \int \!\left[\,\sum_{i\neq j} \kappa_{ij}\,\Omega^{\rm Cone}_{ij} \;-\; \mathcal{F}_{\rm topo} \;-\; \mathcal{E}_{\rm exhaust}\,\right] dt
$$

where $\Omega^{\rm Cone}_{ij}$ is the model's geometric cone-overlap between selection trajectories. For AI alignment this can be explored as an externally defined optimization target over policy and human-behaviour representations. Its application to AI-human alignment is a Tier-3 engineering analogy requiring empirical validation; it does not show that the AI or human implementation instantiates the model's substrate object or settle either party's Level-II status.

**(iv) Map-vs-Territory framing for distribution shift.** V1 §6.3.4's Map–Territory distinction can be used as a structural analogy: the training distribution is the map, the deployment distribution is the territory, and distribution shift measures their mismatch. Continual-learning architectures with explicit feedback loops may outperform fixed-training-distribution alternatives as mismatch grows [Tier 3 — engineering prediction]. Here “computational architecture” is a structural label only; the analogy makes no claim about experience, suffering, or Level II.

**(v) Inattentional-blindness analogy for LLM goal-misgeneralization.** V1 §16.6 uses, as a Tier 4 analogy for inattentional blindness, a mismatch between an Agent's attention vector $\hat{\bf i}$ and the information gradient of the configuration. An LLM can produce fluent text about a prompt's *surface topic* while missing the user's latent intent. This is analogous—not physically identical—to the attention-vector mismatch in V1 §16.6; transformer attention weights (the softmax over context) are not thereby an Agent's intentional vector. The Tier 3 engineering hypothesis is that interventions targeting *attention–intent alignment* (explicit intent elicitation, inference-time redirection) will outperform output-quality-only interventions on preregistered hallucination and goal-misgeneralization benchmarks (e.g. TruthfulQA, HaluEval). No consciousness inference follows [Tier 3 — engineering analogy].

**(vi) Scope boundaries.** Items (i)–(v) are structural engineering analogies, not claims that an AI is or is not a Level-II Agent or moral subject. The computational-architecture label remains a nonphenomenal taxonomy. Candidate DMC or Polaron observables never switch regimes or execute moral status; substrate (Level II) and welfare questions remain open pending the complete physical, phenomenal, and ethical bridges.

The cumulative position is therefore two parallel programs: candidate-substrate research using Protocol A-Prime controls, and structural-alignment engineering for present systems. Both may draw on the same geometric apparatus, but neither supplies a present substrate, Level-II, or moral-patient verdict [Tier 3 — programmatic synthesis].

## Part VI Applications and Extensions

## **PART VI: APPLICATIONS AND OPEN DOMAINS**

### **Introduction to Part VI**

The five preceding Parts of Volume 1 develop a tiered framework for consciousness research. Part I establishes the staircase of certainty and the axiomatic foundation; Part II formalizes the Tri-Partite Ontology of Field $\Psi$, Adelic Solenoid $\Sigma_\infty$, and Agent $\mathcal{F}_{sel}$; Part III proposes the multi-agent Consensus model, the Russellian causal frame, and a Polaron algebraic-unity candidate; Part IV develops candidate bridges to forces and fields; Part V gives a structural account of temporal phenomenology and the exact representation-theoretic decomposition used for Quality Space. Volume 2 extends the framework into cosmic architecture; Volume 3 audits the matter spectrum and the experimental programme. Tier-1 axioms and some Tier-2 geometric results do not close the still-open physical carrier, Selection instrument, clock, transducer, Identity-Polaron realization, owner/subject, or phenomenal bridges; numerical, physical-link, and substrate-specific claims remain Tier 3/Tier 4 targets under the Parameter Ledger.

Part VI is different in kind. The six chapters that follow are *bridging interpretations*. Each takes a formal or phenomenological GCT construct — the proposed coupling matrix $\kappa_{ij}$, the unclosed Selection/phason-drag ansatz, the Class 0 / 1 / 2 taxonomy, the graded (6 linear + 21 quadratic) representation decomposition, or the epistemic tier system — and applies it as a heuristic to sociology, aesthetics, contemplative phenomenology, theology, self-reference, or philosophy of science. These applications neither supply the missing physical or phenomenal bridges nor generate new physics-level predictions from the icosahedral geometry alone.

The calibration anchor for Part VI is the scope position made explicit in V3 §22.9: **GCT offers a proposed ontology and a vocabulary of structural reframing; specific object-level claims in these domains require domain-specific inputs the framework does not generate.** One therefore uses sociological, aesthetic, contemplative, theological, logical, or philosophy-of-science methods to predict outcomes in those disciplines. Part VI may compare beauty with a stipulated coherence surrogate or institutions with a formal $\kappa_{ij}$ network, but those comparisons are interpretive analogies, not evidence for $\eta_{Zeno}$, a physical Identity Polaron, a Selection Operator, an owner or subject count, or GCT validation. A chapter that promised to derive *which* aesthetic preferences a given culture will exhibit, or *which* religious doctrines will achieve institutional stability, would overreach the framework.

**Tier policy for Part VI.** One rule applies uniformly to all six chapters. Exact mathematics cited from Parts I–V keeps its source tier, and no Part VI analogy inherits that tier. Every mapping from a GCT construct into a target domain — sociology, aesthetics, contemplation, theology, self-reference, or lived agency, and whether the proposed bridge is physical or phenomenal — is a **Tier 4 bridge hypothesis**. A claim is labelled **Tier 3** only where an independent, ordinary empirical model carries it (for example a social-dynamics, psychophysical, or cognitive model with its own declared observables and comparison models); the Tier 3 label then belongs to that model, and any GCT reading of it remains Tier 4. Tier 1 appears only where a chapter cites a result that is itself Tier 1 in the original Parts. Purely methodological proposals offered to philosophy of science (Chapter 23) are evaluated as philosophy and carry no physics tier; any GCT-specific reading attached to them is again Tier 4.

The chapters of Part VI address the following topics:

- **Chapter 18 (Social Systems)** — Sociology and institutions as Class-0 social-pattern models with quasi-agency summarised by a phenomenological $\kappa_{ij}$ network; no multi-Polaron or subject derivation is claimed.
- **Chapter 19 (Aesthetics)** — Beauty, musical consonance, and mathematical elegance compared with the icosahedral irrep decomposition as Tier 4 analogies; no substrate mechanism of beauty is claimed.
- **Chapter 20 (Contemplative Practice)** — Cross-tradition phenomenology of meditative and mystical states under the V1 §17.4 states-of-consciousness framework.
- **Chapter 21 (Theology)** — Structural reading of theological vocabulary: soul, God, prayer, grace, sin; religion as institutional Class-0 pattern; compatibility with religious naturalism.
- **Chapter 22 (Strange Loops)** — Hofstadter's strange-loop intuition compared with an algebraic knot candidate and a stipulated unitary/non-unitary boundary; no physical Polaron, Selection Operator, or Gödelian subject-bound is derived.
- **Chapter 23 (Philosophy of Science)** — The epistemic tier system as a portable methodological contribution to philosophy of science; the Russellian causal frame as a contribution to philosophy of causation; the necessity-vs-parsimony question that a completed structural-uniqueness result would raise, with GCT's own icosahedral-selection programme presented as conditional rather than as a completed theorem.

Two structural notes situate Part VI within the broader manuscript. First, the chapters that follow are not derivations. Aesthetic language such as placing octaves and perfect fifths in a low-mismatch region of an auditory $T_1$ coordinate model is a Tier 4 psychophysical proposal; "phason drag" does not name a measured physical interaction or energetic-quale map. Ethnomusicology supplies the empirical inputs, and ordinary acoustic and cultural models remain necessary controls. Second, applied chapters carry weaker physics anchors than Volumes 2 and 3. Their analogies are testable only after their own observables and comparison models are declared; failure or success of an analogy does not by itself falsify or validate GCT, a physical Selection Operator, an Identity Polaron, an owner, or Level II.

The chapters of Part VI are sequenced from the most public domain (social systems) inward through aesthetic, contemplative, and theological phenomenology, then into the formal-logical reframing of self-reference, closing with the philosophy-of-science methodological contribution. The order is conceptual, not dependency-bound; each chapter is self-contained and cross-references Parts I–V where the relied-upon machinery is developed.

### **Chapter 18: Social Systems and Institutions**

This chapter applies the Consensus Protocol of V1 Ch11 — in particular the Class 0 / 1 / 2 entity taxonomy (§11.4, §11.6) and the multi-agent coupling matrix $\kappa_{ij}$ (§11.2) — to the domain of social facts. Under the Part VI tier policy the treatment is a **Tier 3 social model with Tier 4 GCT readings**, not a derivation: the Tier 3 label belongs only to ordinary coarse-grained social-dynamics models with their own observables, and every mapping from GCT constructs onto those models is Tier 4. GCT does not generate which institutions a society will produce or predict a specific revolution, election, or market cycle. Throughout the chapter, *agent* denotes an empirically observed person or functional participant in a social model; it does not assign that person a derived Identity Polaron, physical Selection Operator, owner, or Level-II verdict. Social dynamics require empirically specified communication, incentive, coercion, storage, and transition kernels; Solenoid topology supplies none of them.

---

**18.1 Institutions as Class-0 Patterns with Quasi-Agency**

**18.1.1 The Ontological Question**

Sociology has long faced an ontological question that physical theory has had little to offer on: in what sense do governments, markets, religions, and corporations *exist*? Searle's distinction between "brute facts" and "institutional facts" (constituted by collective intentionality) is the contemporary standard reply; established positions range from Durkheimian social realism (institutions as *sui generis* social objects) to methodological individualism (institutions reducible to the beliefs and actions of their members). The Russellian frame developed in V1 Ch10 and the multi-Polaron Consensus Protocol of V1 Ch11 motivate a conditional structural reading distinct from each of these. [Tier 4 — GCT social-ontology translation]

**18.1.2 The Structural Reading**

An institution — a government, a market, a religion, a corporation — is modeled here as a *high-rigidity Class 0 pattern* physically instantiated in people, artefacts, records, routines, legal dispositions, and communication channels, and maintained by the coordinated activity of its constituent agent network. This classification is structural, not a derived phenomenal verdict: no institution-scale Identity Polaron, Selection-Operator mechanism, spanning unity domain, owner, or phenomenal bridge has been demonstrated, and the Tier-3 Polaron/Level-II bridge remains open for all substrates. The DMC/O.21/O.23/O.34 stack is only one Tier 3 candidate implementation and cannot establish an institutional-scale null. The structural Class-0 label therefore leaves institutional Level II **open (Tier 3)** rather than proved absent: no validated substrate criterion exists yet (it requires a typed, normalized, measured coupling, the Identity-Polaron construction and an independent phenomenal bridge; O.21/O.23/O.34, O.18). The optional Consensus-Action translation represents the network's measured coordination by $\kappa_{ij}$ and its effective pattern by $\Phi_{\mathrm{inst}}$; $\mathcal J[\Phi]$ is then a coarse-grained phenomenological model, not an institution derived from the 6D lattice or the Solenoid. [Tier 4 — GCT Class-0 / $\mathcal J$ mapping onto institutions and its phenomenal interpretation; only an ordinary coarse-grained coordination model with its own observables carries a Tier 3 label]

Throughout this chapter, $\kappa_{ij}$ must therefore be read as a phenomenological social interaction kernel, fitted to data. If one instead adopts the address-based form $\kappa_{ij}=\kappa_0e^{-\lambda_cd_H(i,j)}$, the address filtration, the assignment of addresses to persons, the address-to-coupling law, the exponential form, and $\lambda_c$ are all additional data requiring calibration, and the address-based form is a Tier 4 bridge hypothesis; common-cylinder membership alone has no social causal force.

**18.1.3 What "Quasi-Agency" Means and Does Not Mean**

Institutions exhibit *quasi-agency* because people, rules, records, and enforcement channels jointly produce actions attributed to the collective (a corporation hires, a government taxes, a market clears). This does not imply an institution-level subject. Nor does GCT presently show that individual decisions are produced by physical Selection Operators or coordinated through a multi-Polaron network; in the social model $\kappa_{ij}$ is a Tier 3 social-interaction surrogate, and any reading of it as multi-Polaron coupling is Tier 4. The institution is the *substrate* on which agent-level decisions take coordinated form, not an additional decision-maker layered on top.

This distinguishes the proposed reading from two positions in the social-ontology literature. Against group-mind realism (in which a collective acquires literal mental properties), the present model attributes no aggregate Selection Operator, quale, or Level II subject to the institution absent a separately demonstrated qualified unity domain. Against eliminativist methodological individualism, it treats the institution as *real* because its physically stored rules, resources, role relations, and enforcement channels constrain outcomes even as members change. That persistence depends on ordinary carriers and transmission dynamics, which an explicit physical memory/carrier bridge (not yet constructed) would have to describe; it is not stability conferred by a location, cylinder, or cohomology class in $\Sigma_\infty$. [Tier 3 social model]

**18.1.4 Stability, Decay, and Replacement**

Within the coarse-grained Consensus-Action model, the lifetime of an institutional pattern is modeled through the rate at which physical carriers and the constituent agent network reproduce it. Three useful mechanisms of institutional decay can then be translated as follows; they do not follow from Solenoid topology:

1. *Membership drift.* As highly engaged contributors are replaced by less engaged ones, institutional reproduction may weaken. $\kappa_{ij}$ and $\Phi_{\rm inst}$ are coarse-grained model variables, not rendering pressure. [Tier 3]
2. *Maintenance-cost escalation.* Administrative, material, cognitive, and enforcement costs rise as the institution fits its environment less well; members experience the pattern as increasingly effortful to maintain, which is what is colloquially called institutional sclerosis. [Tier 3] Calling the integrated burden "phason friction" is an optional Tier 4 translation; a physical derivation and calibration would be required before it becomes a measured cost ledger.
3. *Competitive replacement.* A rival pattern may become dominant when enough participants, resources, and enforcement channels shift toward it. Describing this as a lower-$\mathcal J$ consensus minimum is a coarse-grained optimization analogy [Tier 4 — GCT $\mathcal J$ translation], not physical Agent rendering or an energy collapse.

The framework predicts no specific institutional dynamics. A usable model must specify physical and social state variables, the physical carriers of institutional memory, and transition kernels; address nesting supplies none of these.

---

**18.2 Norms and Conventions as Multi-Polaron $\kappa_{ij}$ Equilibria**

**18.2.1 The Persistence Puzzle**

Social norms — traffic conventions, currency acceptance, etiquette, language norms, marriage forms — can persist even when individual deviation would be locally profitable, and can shift in coordinated waves. Game-theoretic accounts treat norms as equilibria of repeated coordination games. GCT proposes an optional translation in which such an equilibrium is represented by a stationary point of the phenomenological Consensus Action Functional of V1 §11.3.1; it does not derive the equilibrium from topology. [Tier 4 — GCT translation]

**18.2.2 The Variational Statement**

Recall from V1 §11.3.2 that the stationarity condition for the consensus potential, in the high-redundancy regime where the entropic correction is suppressed by the total coupling weight, is

$$\Phi_{\text{local}} = \frac{\sum_j \kappa_{ij}\, \Phi_j}{\sum_j \kappa_{ij}}$$

Read as a coarse-grained coordination model, this is the familiar weighted-averaging consensus rule of opinion-dynamics models, and in that ordinary sense a social norm is represented by a region of the effective potential $\Phi$ in which a coordinated practice (drive on the right, accept fiat currency, use this phoneme system) is a local minimum of $\mathcal{J}[\Phi]$ given a calibrated $\kappa_{ij}$ matrix. [Tier 3 — ordinary social-dynamics model] The equation is a model of observed coordination costs. A norm's actual persistence depends on incentives, learning, records, sanctions, network structure, and other physical and social kernels; neither a common address cylinder nor $d_H$ makes it persist.

If a microscopic bridge from agent-level energetic work to the social variables were derived, the model could supply a physical cost ledger rather than merely relabel utility. That bridge is presently open. The comparison between the "weight" of social conformity and Selection-Operator drag against $\Phi_\perp$ (V1 §16.2.3) is therefore a Tier 4 phenomenological translation, not an identity or scale-extension theorem.

**18.2.3 When Norms Change**

Within the coarse-grained potential model, a norm shift is represented when the fitted maintenance cost of the existing equilibrium exceeds the modeled barrier to a competing equilibrium. Three heuristic regimes are useful:

1. *Gradual erosion.* The $\kappa_{ij}$ network supporting the norm decays slowly (members exit, cohorts age out, the pattern stops being transmitted). The norm fades without a discrete transition. [Tier 3]
2. *Coordinated cascade.* A tightly coordinated subnetwork can tip a norm through ordinary organization, communication, and threshold effects. [Tier 3] In the optional super-radiant analogy of V1 §11.8, such a phase-coherent subnetwork is represented by quadratic-in-$N$ rather than linear rendering pressure on a competing $\Phi$ configuration. This scaling is not established for social networks: it requires a defined amplitude, phase observable, and calibrated outcome kernel. [Tier 4 — phenomenological analogy]
3. *Exogenous shock.* An environmental change (technological substrate shift, demographic discontinuity, external coercion) raises the cost of maintaining the existing norm above what any internal-network adjustment can buffer. The norm fails by external loading rather than internal succession. [Tier 3]

In the model, relative support for competing $\Phi$ minima, weighted by the calibrated $\kappa_{ij}$ matrix, is one candidate summary variable. It determines an outcome only inside a validated transition model; the framework neither supplies that kernel nor predicts which regime a given norm-change will follow. [Tier 3]

**18.2.4 Norms versus Institutions**

The boundary between a norm (§18.2) and an institution (§18.1) is not sharp in the model. Both are treated as Class 0 patterns maintained by physical agent networks. The distinction is one of rigidity and codification: an institution typically carries explicit machinery (rules, charters, archives, resources, enforcement) distributed across multiple physical carriers, whereas a norm may rest mainly on tacit coordination. Treating both as Class 0 patterns and calling the former a higher-barrier minimum is a GCT model translation. [Tier 4 — Class-0 / barrier translation; the codification distinction itself is ordinary sociology]

---

**18.3 Revolutions, Phase Transitions, and Reconfiguration Dynamics**

**18.3.1 Revolutions as Consensus De-Rigidification**

In the coarse-grained model, a political revolution may be represented as a phase transition in the physical and social reproduction of an institutional pattern. Below the modeled threshold, the incumbent is a local minimum of $\mathcal{J}[\Phi]$; above it, a rival organization becomes the minimum and the prior pattern loses carriers and enforcement. This is a translation of empirically specified social dynamics, not a transition theorem derived from the Solenoid or the icosahedral lattice. [Tier 3 for an ordinary threshold/phase-transition social model; Tier 4 for its $\mathcal J[\Phi]$ reading]

**18.3.2 Threshold Conditions**

Conditional on the phenomenological potential model, a revolutionary threshold can be sketched as the point where the measured cost of maintaining the incumbent network exceeds the modeled barrier to a competing organization. The physical and social transition kernel must still be supplied. Three candidate factors are:

1. *Internal coherence of the challenger configuration.* A tightly coordinated movement may lower the fitted barrier through ordinary organization and communication. Representing this by $N^2$ super-radiant rendering pressure (V1 §11.8) is a Tier 4 phenomenological analogy that would require a derived amplitude and phase-locking observable; it is not a social scaling theorem.
2. *Decoupling of prevailing enforcement.* If the high-$\kappa_{ij}$ enforcement subnetwork (security forces, key administrators) reduces its coupling to the institutional pattern, the fitted institutional-support variable can fall faster than formal membership alone would suggest.
3. *Exogenous loading.* Famine, war, contagion, technological disruption, or external coercion increase the cost of maintaining the prior pattern.

If a calibrated model shows that the combined loading exceeds its fitted barrier, the consensus may tip toward a new pattern. The framework does not predict *when* this will happen for any specific institution — that is the empirical work of political science and historical sociology — and the listed quantities are candidate observables, not topology-derived sufficient conditions. [Tier 3]

**18.3.3 Post-Revolutionary Reconfiguration**

The aftermath of a phase transition is not the immediate stability of the successor organization. In the coarse-grained potential model, several candidate minima can compete while people, records, resources, and enforcement channels are redistributed. The actual relaxation is governed by the participating agents' physical states and by social transition kernels, not by a trajectory through $\Sigma_\infty$. Historical cases can be described with the multi-basin analogy, but the framework does not generate their mechanisms or outcomes. [Tier 3]

---

**18.4 Distinction from Individualist Consciousness Theories**

Other consciousness theories — Integrated Information Theory (V1 §17.5), Higher-Order Theories (V1 §17.6.3), Global Workspace Theory (V1 §17.6.2), Orchestrated Objective Reduction (V1 §17.6.1) — operate at the level of the individual subject and offer no native machinery for institutional, normative, or revolutionary dynamics. Most are silent on social ontology because their formalism does not extend to it; IIT is the exception, since its exclusion postulate explicitly denies consciousness to aggregates that are not maxima of integrated information.

GCT's multi-Polaron Consensus Protocol supplies a common notation for agents, interaction weights, and coarse-grained patterns. Applying it to institutions is nevertheless an analogy-bearing Tier 4 bridge: a social institution is not thereby the same mathematical object as a microscopic lattice defect (V1 §11.4.1); the common-commutant description of compatible records (V1 §11.13.3; Tier 1 algebra once the updates are supplied, Tier 3 application) does not derive a social equilibrium; and the Polaron algebraic-unity candidate (V1 §11.12) does not derive a revolution. Any claimed scale extension must provide the physical state variables, coarse-graining map, physical carriers of institutional memory, and transition kernels.

The framework's present grip on social ontology is therefore a substrate-compatible vocabulary, not a derivation of institutional existence, persistence, value, or history. [Tier 4 for the GCT reading]

**18.4.1 What This Chapter Does Not Claim**

The chapter offers a structural reframing of social facts within GCT. It does not claim the following:

- It does not derive specific institutions from the icosahedral geometry. Which institutions emerge in a given society is set by historical, ecological, and biographical inputs that the framework does not generate.
- It does not assign Level II apperception to institutions. The structural reading of §18.1 models institutions as Class 0 patterns whose rigidity depends on constituent agents; no institution-scale Selection Operator, owner, phenomenal bridge, or normalized rate pair has been demonstrated. Institutional Level II is therefore **open (Tier 3)** and no $\eta_{Zeno}$ value is assigned; neither is established as zero.
- It does not predict the trajectory of any specific revolution, election, or market cycle. The threshold-condition sketch of §18.3.2 identifies which quantities, in principle, would have to be measured, not what their values are in any historical case.
- It does not derive institutional durability from Solenoid topology. Longevity requires physically persistent records, practices, resources, succession, and transmission channels, described by a physical carrier bridge and a historical transition model.
- It does not derive legitimacy, moral authority, goodness, sinfulness, or any other evaluation from address proximity, nested cylinders, coupling strength, low modeled friction, or longevity. Descriptive persistence and normative warrant are different questions.
- It does not adjudicate among political philosophies. The framework is compatible with liberal, conservative, socialist, and many other first-order political positions; its vocabulary constrains the modeled ontology of institutions, not their evaluation.
